text: In Marshwick, the chair has fallen at every performance since 1904, and the front row now brings cushions for it.
Marshwick swears a goose once walked on mid-wedding, took the bouquet, and was best man at the second one.
In Gloomsby, the candle has gone out at the saddest line since 1962, and the audience applauds it. It is the best-reviewed performer in town.
Gloomsby remembers the night the ghost sheet turned out to have a man named Alfred inside. He had been there since Tuesday.
In Snoring Magna, the curtain stuck halfway in 1961, and the audience slept through the second half without complaint.
Snoring Magna's audience fainted in unison in 1987. The doctor called it a nap. The audience called it a review.
At the Opera House of Wibbling, the chandelier has swung during the second act of every opening night since 1887.
At the Royal Opera House of Wibbling, a prompter once whispered so well that the tenor sang the stage directions. It was acclaimed.
In Hinge Regis, every hero exits through the wrong door, and the audience runs a sweepstake on which one.
Hinge Regis once held a masked ball in a house with four hundred doors. Some guests are, technically, still trying to leave.
In Hemlock Green the corpse always gets up too early, and the gardeners, who know better, tell it to lie back down.
Hemlock Green's cake competition has been cancelled eleven times, always for reasons nobody will put in writing.
Lettersham's postmistress prompts from the front row, loudly, and has never been wrong. Nobody has ever thanked her.
Lettersham once received a parcel marked 'Do Not Open Till Opening Night'. It was a mask. It is still waiting for the face.
In Gandersby, the goose has taken the lead in every pantomime since 1951, and the actors simply work around it.
Gandersby's goose once borrowed the dame's wig, and it was the best-reviewed performance in thirty years.
In Candlewick Down, every kiss on stage is interrupted by a cough, and the cougher has never been found.
Candlewick Down holds that a candle blown out during a wedding scene means forty years of marriage. It is a very smoky town.
In Twelve Bridges, the heroine has leaned left at every performance since the river left, and the bridges lean with her.
At Twelve Bridges, the puppets' strings knot themselves into a bridge during the finale. Nobody has ever tied it deliberately.
Puddlecombe keeps one umbrella on stage for every actor, and it still rains indoors during the second act.
In Puddlecombe, an actor once cried into a watering can, and the audience, being locals, assumed it was weather.
In Pettifog, the court has been staging the wrong play since 1911, and the defence maintains it is better than the right one.
Pettifog once sat through three acts of a villain's apology. The judge fined the villain for brevity.
In Fiddleton, no performance ends in fewer than three encores, and last spring's funeral took five.
Fiddleton's band once rhymed the entire second act in an unrequested key. The audience agreed it was the key.
In Cakeley Wold, the cake in the wedding scene is real, three tiers, and has never survived the interval.
Cakeley Wold's audience once ate the props during a feast scene. The play got a very good review and no ending.
In Grimstone Keep, the swordfight lasts as long as the sword does, which last Tuesday was eleven minutes.
Grimstone Keep has a ghost sheet that appears in Act Two. Nobody remembers hiring it.
In Cragley Steps, the banister has given way at the villain's exit since 1923, and the villain keeps a standing arrangement with a mattress.
In Cragley Steps the chair slides downhill in every drawing-room scene, and the cast now acts at a thirty-degree angle.
In Periwick, the leading man's wig has come off at every opening night since the barbers' strike of 1959.
Periwick once held a masquerade where nobody could tell the masks from the wigs, and the winner was a hat.
In Mooncalf Bay, the paper moon rises early, slips on its string, and every night has to be talked down by the fishermen.
Mooncalf Bay recalls a kiss on the pier so long that the tide came in, went out, and applauded.
In Tinderford, the fire curtain has dropped on every performance since 1938, and the fire brigade holds a seat in the front row.
Tinderford permits one candle per performance. The show with two is remembered, chiefly by the fire brigade.
In Crumbling Upton, the interval pie sells out before the play begins, as it has since 1950, and the pie stall takes the curtain call.
Crumbling Upton's chandelier has been held up since 1903 by one loyal rope, a rumour, and the town's firm belief in it.
In Hullabaloo Gap, the echo returns every line, so the actors learn only half of them. The audience finishes the rest.
Hullabaloo Gap has an echo that rhymes. It started in 1893. The vicar blames the choir.
In Mutterby the audience prompts every line, half a beat early, and the leads wait politely for them to finish.
Mutterby once corrected the cast so thoroughly that the play became a different play. Everyone preferred it.
In Tumbledown Hatch, the trapdoor opens at the finale whether asked or not, and the mayor has long since stopped standing near it.
Tumbledown Hatch has a staircase with no top floor. The banister goes on up into the sky, and the actors go with it.
In Swoonsea, someone faints every quarter hour. The play was written around it, and the pauses are unusually generous.
Swoonsea's lovers kiss, then faint, then wake and kiss the doctor. The doctor had only asked them to breathe.
In Pardonmere, the villain always apologises before the crime, and the victim apologises for being in the way.
Pardonmere's heroes always bump into the wrong door and apologise to it. The door apologises back. It is the town's best scene.
On Sheetley Moor, the ghost sheet has always arrived on cue with a pair of boots showing beneath, and everyone is too polite to say.
On Sheetley Moor they say the candle never goes out until the ghost has finished its line. After that it gets quite rude.
In Couplethwaite, a villain's confession once rhymed all the way to the gallows. He pleaded guilty to the meter.
Couplethwaite's marionettes once knotted their strings into couplets. The puppeteer is still working out the stanza.
In Dewbury, a watering can is presented at the end of every play, and the best actor is watered.
Dewbury's open-air play was rained on in 1988, so the audience held umbrellas over the actors. It remains the finest staging.
Nothing has happened in Grimsditch since 1974 apart from the night the wig came off, which the mayor calls the incident.
In Grimsditch, the corpse once sat up in the third act and was told by the vicar to sit down. It did.
Plover's Rest released a hundred geese in the finale of 1974 and has never mentioned it again.
At Plover's Rest a pigeon has sat in the third row since 1997. The cast bows to it first. It has never asked for an encore.
